notes:
We should build businesses that solve social issues
​
 Summarize
​
Can't solving social problems also be a business?

August 17, 2026
Human Inference is about solving social problems while building a sustainable business with AI.

It’s building in public, not as another tech startup solving a B2B market problem, but as a venture aimed to solve a societal one. It’s lessons about building for non-tech users, on how to solve when the system itself is the problem, while guided by a firm belief shaped by lived experience that what will save us isn’t AI or tech - but what makes us come alive as humans.

You’ll find a home here if you’re tired of working for profit companies that claim to change the world but only within the limits of what their shareholders want.

If you’re an idealist who wants a practical way to make change - real change - that demonstrably improves lives through greater social justice and systemic changes.

You want to improve the world and improve your quality of life at the same time through a business you own, leveraging the latest AI tools or building your own.

That’s what I’m doing here.

I don’t promise to have the answers yet. This isn’t written from the perspective of someone who already had many years of success and forgotten what it’s like to be at the beginning, struggling through the middle, before anything took off.

Instead, you’ll get something better and more useful: A front-row seat experience into seeing someone creating something new, swinging at intractable problems. At how I apply my background in anthropology, business, product, and my lens as someone with ADHD, to problems in a new domain after a decade of success turning around seemingly doomed-to-fail programs in corporate environments.

Where the newsletter began

It didn’t start this way. It began with my first post, “So why write?” I asked if anyone wanted to talk about AI and society:

“Most of my thoughts these days are around - how do we build the kind of world we’d prefer to live in? AI could make it possible - shouldn’t we explore it?”

I didn’t realize how prescient that question was. I also didn’t realize how it would end up defining my journey over the last several months, a journey that began with an odd ache about the things that seemed wrong with the world.



I would call myself apolitical. I do not like engaging in political discussions, which I find full of negativity and confusion in America’s culture. I have always focused on what it meant to live a fulfilling life and was more concerned with having a satisfying career I was proud of.

Breaking the bubble

But the straw that broke the camel’s back came after neighbors’ ACs went out in the Texas heat because of Greystar. I left my apolitical bubble and started looking for real ways to fix broken systems.

Most people can see that a lot is broken about our American system. What’s missing is clear information on what we’re supposed to do about it. I honestly do not think anyone has the answer.

Writers and tech leaders keep asking how we build a better world before AI makes everything worse. They offer thoughtful proposals. Then the conversation usually stops. Having the right idea is treated as enough. The hard part, getting anything real to happen, gets left out.



The 99% market

Tech and venture capital often focuses on high margin opportunities - B2B SaaS and enterprise businesses get most of the attention. What it leaves out of its skyrocketing valuations are all the problems that 99% of the country deeply care about solving: Housing, wealth inequality, generational decline in social mobility.

There’s a deep sense that the system is broken - or worse, rigged. Yet no world-changing startup from the Bay Area seems interested in solving these problems.



There’s a long-standing assumption that civic tech is an unattractive market, and it curbs any would-be entrepreneur from attempting it. But two things are buried in this assumption:

That the only customers are the public institutions. However, these are not the people who are experiencing the pain - it’s the citizens who have the pain and who we should be building for.
What doesn’t interest venture capital is not the same as saying there’s no market. A VC cares more about exiting a unicorn at sky high valuations to cover its portfolio of bets.
We are now also questioning the very need for high upfront capital for many companies. AI-native companies can now operate and build a product at a fraction of the cost. The backlash against AI slop now require community, distribution, and brands to have far more human connection and authenticity to stand out, and these aspects can often be tainted by shareholder interests in many venture backed firms.

I’m leaning in on this crack in the illusion.

I come from a product background with an MBA and training in Anthropology. I have a knack for spotting assumptions and turning failing programs around. I applied those skills to tackling a problem in society - the power of money over American politics, which is eroding our democracy.

It led me to building a voting app to help citizens assess standing members of Congress and candidates based on voting and donation history. My thesis is that we can weaken the relationship between money and who gets elected if voters stopped voting based on what heavily fundraised campaigns pay for.

No voter data will ever be sold to an institution. It is meant to only be a tool that empowers the people who care about democracy the most - its citizens.

It is my current focus for building a business that solves a systemic social problem.

Where the newsletter is heading

Human Inference will chronicle the AI-powered solopreneur journey of blending social change and business models.

The current season is focused on the voting tool and money in politics, but it will also include background on what it takes to build a better society, how can ordinary people take action, and how an entrepreneur with a product and ADHD mind can contribute while simultaneously building a business. Perhaps this journey can serve as an example for others looking for more fulfilling ways to build careers when their values don’t fully align with the conventional professional world.



The name Human Inference describes how I work: I draw from experience, training, a particular brain, and am more apt to trust actual lived human experiences over theories and dead frameworks. It’s from this dataset that I infer what is happening; the human experience, lived and felt, the kind of data that has not been converted into binary and fed into a machine learning training set.

Thanks for reading to the end. I look forward to what’s next and sharing what I find. Help me prove solving social problems can be a business by sharing or subscribing.

# MAGIC (Outcome) Model — notes

*Each thing = a post. 3 things the brain likes.*

## The core question

What's the dream outcome for your customer — and for your audience?

**Dream outcome → Big obstacles → Milestones → Missions**

## Dream outcome / magic moment

No labels, fill your cup — freedom, no fear.
△ = magic moment, then outwards to tactics.

△ mine — Hope, courage — Agency, empowerment to make a difference.

## The obstacle

Big objections / obstacles — what do we help them overcome?

Ex: Imposter syndrome (for empowering leaders)

Undeniable mission — that sense you've got this, to make it happen. *"Doesn't matter, I'll make it happen."*

Opposite pole: Cynicism, despair, overwhelm — *"what can I even do? Unsolvable."*

**Jeremie's** — financial precarity of the middle class → "the opposite of freedom," in our culture, politics, globally.
— Connective, generative, creative, playful as a resistance 🙂

## Milestone

Milestone = what they'd get (by using our product, content, etc.) — the opposite of the obstacle.

Milestones — Agency, hope. What they can do, know the problem, success and learnings.

## Missions

Missions = the process to take from obstacle to the milestone.

Missions (Actionable, short lessons from history, problem → solve in 1 place)

e.g. from imposter syndrome → undeniable mission → master craft, remove resistance, commit to a bold future
↳ many topics in here to form from

((( What they can do to make a difference, understanding the problem (and what works), ex of success

What they can do — 3 missions per milestone.

**Diagram** (Cynicism/Despair/Overwhelm example — this one maps to Voter Choice):

```
        Small wins today (mission)         Ex of success
                    \                          /
              Cynicism -------- Despair
                        \      /
                     (Empowerment) ▲
                          |
                      Overwhelm

        Understand clear simple problem → solve
```

## Testing / funnel

Test it and see what performs well →
Becomes the top of the funnel — you prioritize the area audience is most interested in and can keep the rest.

---

## Applying it — Human Inference

*Working draft, Sept 11, 2026. Obstacles below one at a time; milestones and missions to fill in as we go.*

**Dream outcome:** You're building the future you actually want to live in.

*(Long version: the sense that you're literally building the future and the society you'd prefer to live in — not just changing it, building it.)*

### Obstacle 1 — Overwhelm
*"There's just too much going on, how the hell do we even do this."*

**Milestone (opposite of the obstacle):** Clarity / agency — a sense of "yes, I can do something."

**Missions:**

*The pattern underneath all of these: name the problem simply, then hand over one small, actually-effective lever. Never leave someone at "okay, now what?"*

1. **Start-here kits.** A literal short list — "3 things you can do about X this week." Pure agency, not persuasion: a tool people take and use, not just content they watch.
2. **Myth-busting the complexity itself.** "You've been told this is too complicated to get — here's the actual mechanism, in one minute." Ties straight to the Human Inference thesis: a lot of overwhelm is manufactured complexity, not real complexity.
3. **Hidden leverage reveals.** "You already have more power than you think" — surfacing a lever people don't know exists, smaller and more effective than the "civic duty" version they assume (vote/donate/protest).

Reference/model to reuse: the existing Voter Choice ad concepts (Here's Why → Why Now → Here's How → CTA) — see `Branding/Content/Ideas/How to Build a Better Future with AI.md`. Same shape, applied to Human Inference topics.

### Obstacle 2 — Despair
*Awareness of what's happening, but feeling like there's no point, like nothing can be done.*

**Milestone (opposite of the obstacle):** Hope.

**Missions:**
1. **Proof it's worked before.** History and live, real examples of people actually taking action and succeeding — evidence that hope here isn't naive.
2. **Reframe engagement as a practice, not a bet on one outcome.** Civic engagement is a muscle — stop working it and you lose it, but the fact that you're participating at all *is* the win, not just whatever the final scoreboard says. Focus on the journey/practice, not "we hit this outcome or we failed."
3. **Celebrate participation itself.** Make showing up and staying engaged feel like a real, fun win on its own — not contingent on a specific result.
4. **"Where we've already won" recap.** A running tally of concrete wins — often local/state, not national-news-worthy — that directly counters the "nothing is working" story.
5. **Zoom-local stories.** Pull back from the overwhelming national picture to one hyper-local win or person, so hope feels reachable instead of abstract.
6. **"You're not alone" visibility.** Show how many other people are quietly doing something too (a content version of Voter Choice's Polis-style "who shares your values" viz). Despair often runs on isolation — this counters that directly.
7. *Open thread, not yet solved:* some way to actually show people their past actions had real impact/meaning. Muxin keeps landing on "a tool" for this rather than a content format — worth its own conversation later.

### Obstacle 3 — Outrage
*Anger at the situation, without knowing what to do about it. Activating, but not sustainable.*

**Milestone (opposite of the obstacle):** Joyful creation.

**Missions:**
1. **Empathize first, then redirect.** Validate the anger before doing anything else — "this sucks, I see it, here's exactly what it looks like." Earn trust before pointing anywhere. Then redirect that energy toward pro-social, community-focused action (the same move recovery programs for hate groups/cults use to redirect anger into belonging and purpose — e.g. Life After Hate). Reframe: their anger comes packaged with real understanding of the problem, and that understanding is a genuine asset for change.
2. **Decouple self-worth from the system's scorecard.** Name what's often underneath the outrage: feeling like you're failing by society's terms — can't afford housing, can't start a family — and that the system is rigged and mocking you for it. The way through isn't winning that comparison (some people will always be luckier, whatever the system). It's self-acceptance: your worth was never tied to what the system says you've earned. You can still work to fix a broken system without needing it to deliver you a reward in order to feel whole.
3. **Outrage burns out — creativity and joy sustain.** Outrage is activating but short-term; it's not something to run on long-term. What sustains is creativity, joy, and the felt sense that you're literally building the world you want, bit by bit, every day — not needing one big outcome (win this one election) to validate the work. The practice/participation is the point, and it should feel joyful, not grim.
4. **"What are you building" showcase.** Spotlight regular people mid-practice, enjoying the making itself — modeling joyful creation instead of just telling people to feel it.
5. **Humor/playfulness as resistance.** Satire, absurdity, playfulness that processes the anger without weaponizing it — echoes the earlier "connective, generative, creative, playful as a resistance" line above.
6. **Anger → one act, a ritual.** A short, repeatable practice for taking today's outrage and turning it into one small creative act. More tool than message — pairs well with mission 4.

*(Nuance vs. Despair's "celebrate participation" mission: that one is about the fact that you showed up at all. This one is about how you show up — approaching the work with joy and creativity rather than running on outrage. Related, but distinct.)*

## Six sample Magic Outcome posts

I treated your notes as the sentence bank and added only enough connective tissue to make each post stand alone.

### 1. The problems are huge. Your next move does not have to be.

**Obstacle:** Overwhelm  
**Milestone:** Clarity and agency  
**Mission:** Hidden leverage reveal

**Here’s Why**

When the problems are enormous, it is easy to conclude that nothing we do matters.

But institutions depend on ordinary people for more than we usually acknowledge.

They need our votes.  
They need our labor.  
They need our money.  
They need our attention.  
They need our trust.

And when their systems leave people behind, they still depend on us to care for one another.

**Why Now**

AI is not going to save us if we simply use it to automate the decisions that led us here.

If we want any say in what future gets built, we need to understand what ordinary people actually control.

**Here’s How**

Pick one institution you want to influence and ask three questions:

1. What does it need from people like me?
2. Which of those things can I redirect, withhold, or build with others?
3. What is the smallest real action I can take this week?

Do not start with “How do I fix the world?”

Start with: “What do I control, and what does this system need from me?”

**CTA**

That answer may be the beginning of your power.

---

### 2. Voting is a terrible user experience.

**Obstacle:** Overwhelm  
**Milestone:** Clarity and agency  
**Mission:** Myth-bust the complexity

**Here’s Why**

Think about what we expect a normal voter to do.

Stay on top of political news. Research every candidate. Understand every proposition. Detect misinformation. Make time for the polls.

We would never design a product with this much friction and then blame the user when they dropped out.

Yet that is more or less how we designed democracy.

**Why Now**

Most of us use shortcuts because we have lives.

We recognize a name. We remember an ad. We vote for the party we usually vote for. I have voted based on completely irrelevant factors before, including whether I liked someone’s name.

Campaign money works partly because it pays to make a name familiar.

**Here’s How**

You do not need to become a political expert.

Start with the issues you care about. Then look at what candidates have actually done:

1. How did they vote?
2. Who gave them money?
3. Did their actions support the things you care about?

That is why I built Voter Choice. It does the homework so busy normal people can make their own decision.

**CTA**

Politicians already had the job. You are deciding whether they deserve to keep it.

---

### 3. The breakthrough was not a new protest tactic.

**Obstacle:** Despair  
**Milestone:** Hope  
**Mission:** Proof it has worked before

**Here’s Why**

Every previous plantation strike in Hawai‘i had failed.

Workers were divided by ethnicity, paid differently, housed separately, and used as strikebreakers against one another.

The breakthrough was not a more aggressive protest.

It was a new relationship.

**Why Now**

We often talk about political action as if it means showing up for one march, casting one vote, or producing one dramatic moment.

But people cannot stay in a fight if participating means losing their housing, food, childcare, safety, or community.

**Here’s How**

The ILWU built solidarity into daily life.

Meetings happened across languages. Leadership crossed ethnic groups. During the 1946 strike, people created communal kitchens, fishing crews, transportation, safety patrols, gardens, dances, and alternative banking.

When replacement workers arrived from the Philippines, union members met them at the docks.

They stepped off the ships wearing union buttons.

The systems of care did more than sustain the strike. They broke the dependency the plantation owners used as control.

**CTA**

In a system that uses material vulnerability as power, care is not separate from the strategy.

It may be the strategy.

---

### 4. I thought trying would make the disappointment worse.

**Obstacle:** Despair  
**Milestone:** Hope  
**Mission:** Reframe engagement as a practice

**Here’s Why**

For a long time, I thought there were two ways to respond to a broken world.

Ignore it, or let it consume me.

I assumed that if I tried to make a difference, I would only make the pain worse. There is already so much disappointment in the world. What if I tried and failed?

**Why Now**

It turned out I was making the pain worse by doing nothing.

The professional content I was creating felt like I was holding my breath. Networking events left me empty. I felt like I was living inside a bubble with my head stuck in the sand while the world became more chaotic.

Then I started doing the work I thought was too big, impractical, and probably impossible.

**Here’s How**

I did not suddenly solve anything.

I had conversations. I built a voting tool. I wrote down what I was learning. I found other people who also felt slightly crazy for wanting things to be better.

One day I remembered myself at eleven years old, imagining that I might help society in some way.

I knew that if she could see me now, she would be proud.

That was enough to make the work meaningful before any final outcome arrived.

**CTA**

What did your younger self want to help make better?

You do not have to finish the work this week. You can begin practicing who you wanted to become.

---

### 5. People can use AI every day and still hate what it represents.

**Obstacle:** Outrage  
**Milestone:** Joyful creation  
**Mission:** Empathize first, then redirect

**Here’s Why**

Tech leaders keep treating public anger about AI as job anxiety.

I do not think that fully explains it.

People can use AI at work, recognize its usefulness, and still feel furious about the future being built around it.

Because the question is not only: “Will AI hurt me personally?”

It is also: “Who gets to benefit, who gets hurt, and who gets to decide?”

**Why Now**

A fellow writer looked into buying a small share of upcoming AI-company IPOs.

He was locked out before he could make the purchase. The message said he needed at least $500,000 in investable assets first.

Most people are being told to adapt faster, work harder, and prepare for disruption while the most valuable opportunities remain reserved for people who already have wealth.

People do not object to someone else winning.

They object when the game no longer feels fair enough for everyone to participate.

**Here’s How**

Anger often contains a real understanding of the problem.

Write down exactly what feels unfair. Then ask:

1. What rule or incentive creates it?
2. Who benefits from that rule?
3. What could make that mechanism visible, weaker, or easier to challenge?

That question led me to build a tool that looks at what politicians did and who funded them, instead of asking voters to trust another campaign promise.

**CTA**

What part of your anger is information?

And what could you build from it?

---

### 6. My anxiety is a tiny rain frog.

**Obstacle:** Outrage  
**Milestone:** Joyful creation  
**Mission:** Anger into one act, as a ritual

**Here’s Why**

Fear and anger can be useful signals.

They are terrible project managers.

Whenever I focused too much on outcomes, I would get pulled into someone else’s bag of magic tricks. I would doubt everything, change direction, and spend less time on the writing and building I actually cared about.

**Why Now**

Outrage can activate us, but it cannot sustain us.

The work lasts when it contains expression, play, curiosity, and some enjoyment of making the thing itself.

I started imagining my anxious mind as a tiny rain frog screaming into the air.

It is ridiculous enough to help.

**Here’s How**

When the frog starts yelling:

1. Let it have its say.
2. Ask what it noticed that matters.
3. Turn that information into one small creative act.
4. Pat it on the head.
5. Do the thing you were going to do anyway.

Write one paragraph. Make one introduction. Check one representative’s record. Draw the absurdity. Build the smallest useful version.

**CTA**

Your anger does not need to disappear before you act.

It just does not need to drive.

## What I would test first

For the cleanest initial test, publish one mission from each obstacle:

1. **Overwhelm:** “The problems are huge. Your next move does not have to be.”
2. **Despair:** “I thought trying would make the disappointment worse.”
3. **Outrage:** “My anxiety is a tiny rain frog.”

Those three isolate the emotional promise cleanly: agency, hope, and joyful creation. Then test the more evidence-heavy versions, especially Hawai‘i, voting UX, and AI fairness, against whichever emotional branch receives the strongest response.

Historical facts, election claims, and quantitative details should get a fresh source check immediately before publication. The personal pieces and the ordinary-power map are the safest drafts to test first.

# Cleaned versions to Post

---

When the problems are enormous, it’s easy to conclude that nothing we do matters.

But institutions depend on ordinary people for more than we usually acknowledge. They need our votes, labor, money, attention, trust, and our willingness to care for one another when their systems leave people behind.

None of those things fixes everything. They’re simply places where we are not powerless.

When I wanted to do something about money in politics, I built Voter Choice so people could look at how their representatives actually voted without doing hours of research.

When I started talking to people working on democracy, I found people with projects that needed skills someone else had. I began connecting them instead of trying to get everyone to agree on one big project.

Even buying groceries can be a choice. I buy expensive pasture-raised eggs because I want to support independent farmers, regenerative agriculture, and happy hens. Have you seen how cute they are?

If you want to do something right now, use [Voter Choice](https://voterchoice.vote/) to check one representative on one issue. Or introduce two people who should know each other. Or redirect one purchase you were already going to make.

Choose whatever is easiest.

I wrote a fuller map of these options in [The world’s broken. What do we do?](https://www.humaninference.ai/essays/the-worlds-broken-what-do-we-do)

---

Voting is a terrible user experience.

Think about what we expect a normal voter to do: Keep up with political news, research every candidate, understand every proposition, detect misinformation, and then make time to stand in line.

We would never design a product with this much friction and then blame the user when they dropped out.

Most of us use shortcuts because we have lives. We recognize a name. We remember an ad. We vote for the party we usually vote for.

I have voted based on completely irrelevant factors before, including whether I liked someone’s name.

You don’t need to research your whole ballot today.

Open [Voter Choice](https://voterchoice.vote/), enter your registered address, and click “Pull my representatives.” Choose one issue you already care about and look at how one person actually voted.

Start with the person who already has the job.

You’re paying tax dollars for them to do it. Wouldn’t you want to see what they’ve done before handing it to them again?

Every previous plantation strike in Hawai‘i had failed.

Workers were divided by ethnicity, paid differently, housed separately, and used as strikebreakers against one another.

The breakthrough wasn’t a better protest tactic. It was the relationships workers had built.

The ILWU organized across ethnic groups and languages. During the 1946 strike, people created communal kitchens, fishing crews, transportation, safety patrols, gardens, dances, and alternative banking.

When replacement workers arrived from the Philippines, union members met them at the docks.

They stepped off the ships wearing union buttons.

The systems of care did more than sustain the strike. They broke the dependency plantation owners had used to control people.

I’m not organizing a strike, but I ran into a much smaller version of this while facilitating a democracy group. Trying to get thirteen people with different ideas to agree on one big project produced very little. Looking for two people with something useful to offer each other was much easier.

If a project you care about is missing a skill, open your contacts and find one person who might have it. Send them this:

“I’m working on [specific thing], and I think your experience with [specific skill] could help. Would you have twenty minutes to help me think through one next step?”

You don’t need to assemble a movement. You can start with one useful conversation.

The Hawai‘i story and the research behind it are in [The world’s broken. What do we do?](https://www.humaninference.ai/essays/the-worlds-broken-what-do-we-do). I’m collecting more of what I learn about collective action on my [Actions page](https://www.humaninference.ai/actions).

---

I used to think there were two ways to respond to a broken world: Ignore it, or let it consume me.

I assumed that trying to make a difference would only make the disappointment worse. There is already so much wrong. What if I tried and failed?

It turned out I was making the pain worse by doing nothing.

The professional content I was creating felt like I was holding my breath. Networking events left me empty. I felt like I was living inside a bubble with my head stuck in the sand while the world became more chaotic.

Then I gave myself three months to treat the work I actually cared about as an experiment.

I didn’t suddenly solve anything. I had conversations, built a voting tool, and wrote down what I was learning.

One day I remembered myself at eleven years old, imagining that I might help society in some way. I knew that if she could see me now, she would be proud.

If you have fifteen minutes today, open whatever notes app you already use and finish this sentence:

“If my eleven-year-old self could watch what I did for the next fifteen minutes, she would be proud to see me…”

Set a timer and do whatever you wrote.

If nothing comes to mind, borrow something I did: Send a useful tool to one person, schedule one conversation about something you care about, or check how one representative voted.

I wrote more about this in [Don’t Read if You’d Rather Burn Out Early](https://www.humaninference.ai/essays/dont-read-if-youd-rather-burn-out-early).

---

People can use AI every day and still hate what it represents.

Tech leaders often treat public anger about AI as fear of losing jobs. I don’t think that fully explains it.

People can recognize that AI is useful while feeling furious about the future being built around it.

A fellow writer looked into buying a small share of upcoming AI-company IPOs. He was blocked because he didn’t have at least $500,000 in investable assets.

Most people are being told to adapt faster, work harder, and prepare for disruption while some of the biggest opportunities remain reserved for people who already have wealth.

That’s why I keep coming back to fairness.

People don’t care that someone else has more. They care that the rules feel rigged and there is no longer a game everyone gets to participate in.

Thinking about the whole economic system doesn’t give me anything useful to do before lunch. Looking at one person with political power does.

If money in politics is part of what makes you angry, open [Voter Choice](https://voterchoice.vote/). Enter your registered address, choose one issue, and check how one representative voted and who funded them.

Don’t research everyone. Check one person who currently has power over your life.

I explored more of the fairness underneath the AI backlash in [Why Do Americans Hate AI?](https://www.humaninference.ai/essays/why-do-americans-hate-ai).

---

Whenever my mind starts screaming about everything that could go wrong, I picture a tiny rain frog.

It started when I was spending too much time thinking about whether my work would succeed.

Whenever the numbers weren’t moving, I would find another business guru with a bag of magic tricks. Then I’d spend days questioning everything and less time on the writing and building I should have been doing.

I started treating the anxious part of my mind like a tiny frog screaming into the air.

I can let it have its say, pat it on the head, thank it for its input, and do the thing I was going to do anyway.

If your own frog is loud today, give it one minute. Write down what it’s yelling about.

Then set a ten-minute timer and open the thing you already know you care about.

For me, that usually means opening the draft or terminal I’ve been avoiding and working on it until the timer ends. If what’s bothering you is political, [Voter Choice](https://voterchoice.vote/) gives you something equally small: Enter your address, choose one issue, and check one person’s record.

The frog doesn’t have to go away first.

There’s more about how I ended up using this in [Don’t Read if You’d Rather Burn Out Early](https://www.humaninference.ai/essays/dont-read-if-youd-rather-burn-out-early).

3. Simple start-here checklists: turn your “3 things you can do about X this week” idea into something readers can use.

My recommendation is to try short written posts first, because you already have substantial written material. That is a suggestion, not a commitment to a platform or paid product.

Which of these feels easiest and most enjoyable for you to make regularly?

I just feel like I have nothing to bounce off of and nothing to feed off of or build off of really if I don't have something to talk with. And I'm just talking to a camera. Does that help? I already do have a lot of written material and I do believe that all those accounts are connected, especially GitHub, especially LinkedIn, Substack, some X that you could use as an initial analysis of what's working and what's not. I also don't mind generating images. I just don't find it as easy as writing.

Yes, that helps. Writing is your natural medium, including longer pieces. Video works better for you when there is someone to respond to, so recorded conversations could remain an occasional option. Images sound like an optional addition too.

Your existing posts could provide a useful baseline, though connected accounts alone don't tell us what's working. We haven't established those results yet.

Over the next 14 days, how much time would feel comfortable to spend writing and sharing your work?

That gives us a useful boundary: a few hours a week for writing and sharing, with up to eight available if needed, alongside your software work. Since writing comes naturally and you already have material, short posts drawn from that material seem like a manageable starting point.

What would make the next 14 days feel worth continuing: readers describing how something helped them, more people subscribing or trying your tool, or finding a writing rhythm you enjoy? I’d lean toward useful reader responses alongside an enjoyable rhythm, because those would help you judge both whether the work helps people and whether you want to keep making it.

I would really like to see some numbers move. Growth and subscribers, some actual leads, some actual sales. I really need to solve for income. That's what's making me the most Asians right now. I think you are right about the enjoyable rhythm and useful reader responses, however, because those are very important early signals as well.

Yes. Income is the pressing need, so an enjoyable rhythm and useful reader responses are early signals, while subscriber growth, leads, and sales are the business outcomes you want to see. We should connect your writing to a clear opportunity to earn before agreeing on numerical targets. What, if anything, can someone pay you for today?

Yes, that helps. You want income from things you create, and managing clients would pull you away from that. Consulting remains a fallback you might consider, not your preferred business.

Three possibilities fit what you’ve described:

2. A short book or practical guide: turn one focused part of your existing material into something people can buy once. It has a clearer finish line, though we still need evidence of what readers would pay for.

I’d explore a focused guide first because it uses your existing writing and gives you a bounded product to test. That is a proposal, not a decision or a promise of quick income.

analysis.reply:
Human Inference will test whether content helps people move from overwhelm to agency, despair to hope, and outrage to joyful creation. The initial evidence will be meaningful responses and converted funnel behavior, including essay clicks, signups, survey responses, requests, leads, and eventually sales. The first six posts are defined but not yet scheduled. Paid offers and ongoing publishing pace remain open.

Your interview context is complete and ready for closeout review. Review it below, then choose Start venture to record it and open your Venture workspace. Nothing publishes or becomes a phase approval.

fields.text:
Human Inference helps people build the future they want to live in:
 overwhelm → clarity and agency, despair → hope, outrage → joyful creation.
evidence:
Human Inference helps people build the future they want to live in:
 overwhelm → clarity and agency, despair → hope, outrage → joyful creation.

fields.text: Voters in America
evidence: Voters in America

fields.text: They know the system is broken but don't know what to do about it
evidence: They know the system is broken but don't know what to do about it

fields.text: The system creates manufactured complexity and leaves ordinary people without clear, practical levers for action.
evidence: What’s missing is clear information on what we’re supposed to do about it.

fields.text: If this works, readers move from overwhelm, despair, or outrage toward clarity, agency, hope, and joyful creation, including taking a meaningful concrete action.
evidence: how it needs thriving, joyful experience rather than just outrage

fields.text: You have built and tested Voter Choice, created a private local dictation tool you use daily, and developed substantial writing and software projects.
evidence: I did recently launch a local dictation tool that runs on your Mac, uses free models, and it's completely private.
It is my current focus for building a business that solves a systemic social problem.

fields.text: People have expressed excitement and support for the vision of Voter Choice, but there is not yet evidence of product use, paid demand, or sustained behavior.
evidence: people are very excited and are very supportive of the vision whenever to give me user feedback
I haven't actually launched it yet

fields.text: People have thanked you for writing about how not to burn out and how to sustain joyful social work. People have also responded positively to the Voter Choice vision, but no product use or paid demand is established.
evidence: People have thanked me before in sub stack for talking about the how not to get burnt out or how to stay alive while doing the type of work that we're trying to do
Other people have thanked me for building the voting tool every time I've asked for feedback.

fields.text: You combine anthropology, business, product, and lived experience with ADHD to spot assumptions and turn around difficult programs.
evidence: I come from a product background with an MBA and training in Anthropology.
I have a knack for spotting assumptions and turning failing programs around.

fields.text: Continue using concrete personal experience, demonstrations, historical examples, and practical tools as proof-bearing material. Audience response remains the evidence to preserve and reuse.
evidence: The most surprising material is the combination of the Hawai‘i strike, the tiny rain frog, the elderly neighbor, and your 11-year-old self.

fields.text: They feel overwhelmed by how much is broken and unsure how to act.
evidence: There's just too much going on, how the hell do we even do this.
Cynicism, despair, overwhelm

fields.text: They waste time trying to understand complex systems, politics, candidates, and what actions might actually help.
evidence: People are expected to follow political news, evaluate every race, and find time to vote.

fields.text: They do not trust shareholder-driven claims of social change, opaque systems, or complexity without practical action.
evidence: Having the right idea is treated as enough.

fields.text: They want to make a meaningful difference but keep postponing action because the problems feel too large or unsolvable.
evidence: What they can do to make a difference, understanding the problem (and what works), ex of success

fields.text: Their language includes “everything feels broken,” “what can I even do,” and feeling “alone or crazy for trying.”
evidence: Everything feels broken
what can I even do? Unsolvable.
Feel alone or crazy for trying

fields.text: Writing, including short and longer written posts, feels most natural. Video is easier when it is an interview or live conversation. Images are possible but less easy.
evidence: Short written posts are the easiest for me. That's the media, even longer written posts, but writing is the most natural fitting for me.
I can really reliably create a video is just by recording an interview or a conversation I'm having with somebody live.
I also don't mind generating images. I just don't find it as easy as writing.

fields.text: A short written post drawn from existing material.
evidence: Short written posts are the easiest for me.

fields.text: Substack is the current primary home for the writing, but whether it is the best place to grow remains unknown.
evidence: My primary home has been sub-sac. However, I do not know if it's the best place to grow.

fields.text: Monologue-style video, especially staring at a screen and talking to a camera.
evidence: I'm just talking to a camera.

fields.text: A few hours a week feels definitely possible, with up to eight hours available if needed, alongside software work.
evidence: at least a few hours a week is definitely possible. Maybe up to eight if I need to.

fields.text: The current monetization hypothesis is a free-core, premium-subscription version of Voter Choice. Other possibilities remain open, including paid writing, books, and productized tools.
evidence: I'm planning on making it free for the core flow, but selling a premium subscription product.

fields.text: A person can take one small, concrete civic or creative action, such as checking one representative, making one introduction, or completing one short exercise.
evidence: Choose whatever is easiest.
Set a timer and do whatever you wrote.

fields.text: A meaningful one- or two-week win is a reader moving through the funnel and, where relevant, taking one concrete civic or creative action. The specific action may include using Voter Choice, while the exact offer remains open.
evidence: I suppose that might be the voting app itself
it would be based on the type of responses we get from people, but also based on the data
how much did it go through the funnel?

fields.text: The business should not become primarily client-management or consulting work.
evidence: I just don't like the idea of managing clients and helping them solve their own problems.

fields.text: The first 14 days should show movement in subscribers, growth, leads, or sales while also producing useful reader responses and an enjoyable writing rhythm.
evidence: I would really like to see some numbers move. Growth and subscribers, some actual leads, some actual sales.

fields.text:
Can't solving social problems also be a business?
The problems are huge. Your next move does not have to be.
Voting is a terrible user experience.
evidence: Can't solving social problems also be a business?
The problems are huge. Your next move does not have to be.
Voting is a terrible user experience.

fields.text: What will save us isn’t AI or tech, but what makes us come alive as humans.
evidence: what will save us isn’t AI or tech - but what makes us come alive as humans.

fields.text:
“What can I control, and what does this system need from me?”
“Serious ≠ solemn.”
“Indignation metabolized into engineering.”
evidence: What do I control, and what does this system need from me?
Serious ≠ solemn
Indignation metabolized into engineering

fields.text: Avoid solemnity and dismalness; use humor, playfulness, and human connection when appropriate.
evidence: do it in a way that's kind of funny so that's not so like dismal.
Serious ≠ solemn
I've scheduled out the six posts that we created from the magic outcome notes.

fields.text: Six posts define the initial test. Ongoing pace is explicitly deferred until the test results are reviewed; the content studio is intended to manage cross-platform production.
evidence: I've scheduled out the six posts that we created from the magic outcome notes.
Part of the whole reason we even have this content studio system is so that it can create a bunch of posts for me across a lot of different platforms

fields.text: No vanity-view target selected. Track qualified clicks through to essay reading, signup, survey response, request, lead, and sale as funnel diagnostics.
evidence: let's skip Vanity Metrics.
how many people actually clicked on that?
Like how much did it go through the funnel?

fields.text: No numeric opt-in target selected yet; signups and survey responses will be tracked as baseline funnel behavior.
evidence: So we have survey responses and signups and essay visits, but we don't have requests, leads, and sales.

fields.text: A useful response describes how a mission helped, identifies a concrete need, or asks for specific further help.
evidence: Yes, I think so.

fields.text: An enjoyable writing rhythm and useful reader responses are important early signals of sustainability.
evidence: I think you are right about the enjoyable rhythm and useful reader responses, however, because those are very important early signals as well.
